title: fix/1294_exhaustive-clear-sequenceDb-variables
body:
## :bookmark_tabs: Summary

Reason of bugs like one in issue are global variables cached between renders. I've made exhaustive cleanup of sequenceDb.

You can reproduce the bug in [mermaid live editor](https://mermaid.live/edit) with these diagrams:

```mermaid-example
sequenceDiagram
    Alice->>Bob: Hello Bob, how are you ?
    Bob->>Alice: Fine, thank you. And you?
    create participant Carl
    Alice->>Carl: Hi Carl!
    create actor D as Donald
    Carl->>D: Hi!
    destroy Carl
    Alice-xCarl: We are too many
    destroy Bo
    Bob->>Alice: I agree
```

```mermaid-example
sequenceDiagram
    Alice->>Bob: Hello Bob, how are you ?
    Bob->>Alice: Fine, thank you. And you?
    create participant Carl
    Alice->>Carl: Hi Carl!
    create actor D as Donald
    Carl->>D: Hi!
    destroy Carl
    Alice-xCarl: We are too many
    destroy Bob
    Bob->>Alice: I agree
```

Resolves [#1294](https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid-live-editor/issues/1294)

## :straight_ruler: Design Decisions

I've added imperative state. It's simple structure, that is created from init function and provides reset method, that recalls init function to restore initial values of state's fields. This approach ensures that newly added state fields are cleared.

Also I've added two identity functions, that help specify type of state initial values for typescript.

```suggestion
#### Unfixable actor/participant creation/deletion error

If an error of the following type occurs when creating or deleting an actor/participant:

> The destroyed participant **participant-name** does not have an associated destroying message after its declaration. Please check the sequence diagram.

And fixing diagram code does not get rid of this error and rendering of all other diagrams results in the same error, then you need to update the mermaid version to (v<MERMAID_RELEASE_VERSION>+).

```

comments.author: aloisklink
rflban
comments.body: I've replace cif with assert, but this way is not strict enough. For example, it's possible: `const value = {} as string;`. Constrained identity functions are commonly used in functional typescript and modern javascript engines can inline functions like this one.

comments.author: aloisklink
comments.body:
Hmmm, TypeScript does throw an error if the object is not empty, like `const value = {hi: 1} as string; // TypeScript error`.

> modern javascript engines can inline functions

That's a good point! Although, as a browser-based library, we also need to worry about about size and initial parsing/compile times.

To be honest, I'm still not fully convinced that CIFs are a good fit for this project, but I'm not super experienced with TypeScript. Maybe it makes sense for more complicated use-cases? Well, how it is currently works fines, so we can always decide on using CIFs in the future. We still have a bunch of JS files to convert to TS too :)
